description: We arWe are AetherMind, a team of students passionate about space, technology, AI, and innovation. We combine software development, data analysis, visualization, and creative problem-solving to build impactful solutions for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We welcome curious and motivated teammates interested in AI/ML, software, data science, design, Earth and space sciences, and communication. Let’s create what’s next!
summary: AetherMind is a static, accessible web dashboard that helps students and curious readers explore NASA microgravity combustion research. It presents three NASA studies: Saffire VI (spacecraft-scale fire on a Cygnus vehicle), FLEX (cool flames discovered on the International Space Station), and SoFIE-MIST (ignition and extinction of a solid fuel in microgravity). Users pick a topic (Smoke Detection, Extinction, or Material Flammability) and the studies are reordered by transparent, fixed rules: 2 points if the source directly addresses the topic, 1 if it only mentions it as context, 0 if not mentioned. A side-by-side comparison tool shows what each study examined and under which conditions, and says "Not reported in this source" instead of guessing. Every finding links back to its NASA page. This addresses the challenge by turning dense technical sources into clear, honest, navigable summaries without inventing results, safety advice, or risk scores. It matters because understanding how fire behaves in space is essential for spacecraft safety, and clear access to that knowledge helps more people learn from it.
details:
What it does: Flame in Freefall lets users choose one of three topics (Smoke Detection, Extinction, Material Flammability) and explore three NASA microgravity combustion studies ordered by relevance to that topic. Each study card shows what was studied, the reported finding (or stated objective when no results exist), the experimental context, a short interpretation, and a link to the NASA source. A comparison tool puts any two studies side by side (platform, material, flow, oxygen, pressure, fuel). Where a source does not give a detail, the page says "Not reported in this source".

How it works: The page uses fixed, transparent rules rather than live AI. Each study gets 2 points if its reported finding or objective directly addresses the topic, 1 if the topic appears only as context, and 0 if not mentioned. Higher scores come first and ties keep the original order. The points are only a sorting aid, not a measure of importance, safety, or risk.

Benefits and intended impact: Technical NASA sources are hard for students and general readers to navigate. Our dashboard makes them approachable while staying faithful to the sources. We clearly label preliminary results (e.g., Saffire VI is one test with one material) and objectives (SoFIE-MIST has no results yet), so users do not over-generalize. Understanding fire behavior in microgravity supports spacecraft safety, and we hope the tool encourages readers to open and read the NASA sources directly.

Tools: HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript in a single static file, no external libraries or tracking. Code and AI-assisted summaries were drafted with Claude (Anthropic, Claude Sonnet 5.5) and checked by our team against the linked NASA pages.

Creativity: Instead of a black-box AI ranking, we made the logic fully explainable and visible on the page. The tool prioritizes honesty ("Not reported" instead of guessing).

Factors considered: Accuracy, avoiding safety claims or risk scores, accessibility (keyboard navigation, visible focus states, large touch targets, sufficient contrast, reduced-motion support, responsive layout), and clear SI disclosure. This is an unofficial student project, not endorsed by NASA.
